description: Hello, we are the Oriyon technology team. We are implementing a project as part of the "Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions" competition at the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.
summary: Kisht is a decision-support tool for the NASA Space Apps challenge Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data. A farmer outlines a field, chooses a crop, a sowing date, a soil class, an irrigation method and how much water is available each week. Kisht places NASA POWER daily weather on those sowing dates and calculates a day-by-day FAO-56 water balance. NASA SRTM elevation is used for the field surface. The farmer can compare sowing dates across five historical POWER years, and can order a three-season crop sequence by water, by a soil-sequence index, or by the gaps between crops. Each day the screen states whether water, heat or cold is the signal, and why. If drought, cold or heat crosses a stated scenario line, the pictured crop stops growing and the page explains the cause. Kisht does not calculate yield, disease, nitrogen or organic matter. Soil marked unknown is treated as loam. POWER is regional reanalysis, not a sensor on the field. The result is a scenario to discuss with a local agronomist, not a prescription.
details:
Kisht helps a farmer test a field plan against NASA weather before the season. The farmer outlines a field, chooses a crop, a sowing date, a soil class, an irrigation method, a weekly water limit and an irrigation calendar. Kisht loads NASA POWER for a matching historical year and places that weather on the sowing dates. When a POWER day has the inputs required for FAO-56, crop water use is reference evapotranspiration times a single crop coefficient. Rain the soil cannot take in does not fill the root zone. Each day shows storage, uptake, unmet demand, rain, irrigation, and whether water, heat or cold is the signal.

SRTM elevation shapes the field surface. The plants are a picture of the calculation. A separate Demo tab uses synthetic weather and is labeled as a teaching example. It is not the farmer’s field and not a NASA observation.

The farmer can compare sowing dates across five POWER years, 2020–2024. Plans are ordered by completed seasons, then by fewer frost days, fewer heat days, less unmet demand, and a smaller shift from the farmer’s own date. A three-season sequence can be ordered by water, by a soil-sequence index, or by gaps between crops. The index starts at 100, subtracts points for a repeated crop family, adds points for a legume or alfalfa season, and subtracts points for a gap beyond 180 days. It compares plans. It does not measure nitrogen, organic matter or erosion.

Thirteen crops use published FAO-56 stage and coefficient profiles, not local cultivars. A generic legume is only an illustration. Unknown soil is treated as loam. Rice is not modeled as a flooded field. If drought, cold or heat crosses a stated scenario line, the pictured crop stops growing and the page gives the reason. That stop is a scenario rule, not a measured cultivar death and not a yield.

The intended benefit is a clearer season plan: the farmer can see which days are short of water, hot or cold, compare a sowing date, and discuss a rotation with a local agronomist. Kisht does not promise yield, income, disease control or a prescription.

The site is built with React, TypeScript and Vite. The field view uses Three.js. The map uses Leaflet. Live app: https://kisht-nine.vercel.app
 Code: https://github.com/tuhtaevsalmon/kisht
Super Intelligence tools used to help write and review the application were Claude-sonnet 5, GPT-Astra, Kimi 3.1 Pro and Grok 4.7. They do not calculate the water balance, the risk days or the rotation scores. An optional in-app assistant uses Google Gemini only to explain the current field and propose inputs. If Gemini is not configured, that assistant is off and the rest of Kisht still runs.
